name: Thermal Processing vs. Washing for Cyclospora Produce Safety
anchorClaim: Thermal processing of fresh agricultural produce (encompassing all varieties of fruits and vegetables), specifically achieving a sustained internal temperature of at least 158°F (70°C) for a minimum of 2 minutes, achieves a >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts, whereas applying the maximum standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fails to achieve even a 99% (2-log) reduction on those same items.
plainQuestion: Heating produce to a safe cooking temperature kills Cyclospora, a parasite that causes serious diarrheal illness, better than washing does.
confidenceSummary: The Grade F is a caution about quality: only a handful of the studies reviewed tested Cyclospora itself, the rest studied related parasites or a lab stand-in organism, and much of the direct evidence traces back to a single research group.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 9 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 5 (56%) support the idea that heating produce to a safe cooking temperature kills Cyclospora better than washing does; 4 (44%) point the other way. So the clear findings lean toward the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade F beside it matters just as much: this is a weak and thin evidence base, so treat it as an early signal rather than a settled result. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
DATOM gives this claim a confidence score of 23%, which falls in the "Speculative" band. That is well below the 19% of evidence that directly supports the claim head-on, because confidence measures more than a simple vote count. It also measures how strong, how current, and how independent the evidence actually is, and on all three counts, this evidence base has real gaps.

Start with directness: only 16 of the 54 pieces of evidence (30%) actually tested Cyclospora cayetanensis. The other 38 (70%) are conditional by nature, since they tested a different pathogen or a stand-in organism instead of the parasite the claim is actually about.

Then there is how current the direct evidence is. The strongest, most exact match for the claim's numbers, the 2017 Ortega and Robertson paper, largely restates experimental findings the same small research group published in 2006, 2008, and 2014. In fact, Ynés R. Ortega appears as an author on 8 of the 54 pieces of evidence (15%), spanning 1997 through 2017. No independent research group appears to have repeated or re-tested these exact Cyclospora thermal and washing numbers since 2017, so this is a small, aging, and not fully independent body of direct evidence, even though it points in one consistent direction.

Sample size reporting is a real problem across the board. 35 of the 54 pieces of evidence (65%) list their sample size as "Not reported." DATOM's own scoring flags 45 of the 54 (83%) with a sample-size issue serious enough to question how much weight the result can carry, including 9 pieces of evidence with such a small number of samples that a single unusual result could change the entire finding. Only 9 of the 54 (17%) are confirmed as adequately or well powered.

The evidence is also spread thin across methods: 44 different research methodologies appear across the 54 pieces of evidence, which means almost no two studies did the same experiment the same way. That wide spread makes it hard for any single finding to be independently confirmed by a second, differently designed study. On top of that, 37 of the 54 (69%) are extracted as text only, without the full original paper attached, versus 17 (31%) with the full paper reviewed, and none of the 54 have their journal name on file, so more than two thirds of this evidence base cannot currently be double-checked against the original document.

Put it together: a real, one-sided lean toward the claim within the Cyclospora-specific evidence, but that evidence is a minority of the total, comes largely from one research group's work over two decades, and much of the wider supporting evidence is small in scale, unreplicated, and hard to independently verify. That combination earns a "Speculative" score, even though outright contradiction of the Cyclospora-specific numbers is absent.
decisionSupport: The evidence that directly tested Cyclospora cayetanensis leans one-sided: of the 16 pieces of evidence (30% of the total) that actually studied this parasite, 7 support the claim and 9 support it only under specific conditions, and none contradict it. But DATOM's overall confidence score is just 23% ("Speculative"), so treat the claim as a reasonable starting assumption, not a settled fact.

Much of the strongest direct evidence traces back to one research group. Ynés R. Ortega is an author on 8 of the 54 pieces of evidence (15%), published between 1997 and 2017, and no independent group appears to have re-tested these exact numbers since 2017. Look for newer, independent confirmation before treating the 70°C for 2 minutes and 99.9% inactivation figures as fully settled.

Most of this evidence base, 38 of 54 pieces of evidence (70%), did not study Cyclospora at all. It studied other bacteria, viruses, or a stand-in parasite used because Cyclospora cannot be grown in a lab. That evidence is broadly consistent with heat working better than washing, but it cannot prove the exact Cyclospora numbers in the claim.

Do not assume ordinary home washing is protective against this kind of parasite. One study found that even a strong tap-water flow only reduced bacteria on lettuce by about 80% (0.9-log), and a separate study found that a similarly hardy parasite, Giardia lamblia, persisted in 11 to 33% of samples even after washing eliminated detectable E. coli.

Before relying on this for any food-safety decision, check the original sources directly. 35 of the 54 pieces of evidence (65%) do not report a sample size, 37 (69%) are extracted as text summaries without the full original paper attached, and none of the 54 have journal information on file, so the underlying studies should be looked up directly rather than trusted from the extracted summary alone.
guide.faultLines:
Most of the Direct Evidence Comes From One Research Group, and It Is Getting Old: the clearest match for the claim's exact numbers is a 2017 paper by Ynés R. Ortega and Lucy J. Robertson, but Ortega is also an author on 7 other pieces of evidence in this set, dating back to 1997. That is 8 of the 54 (15%) tracing to one overlapping group of researchers across two decades. No independent lab appears to have re-tested these exact 70°C, 2 minute, 99.9% inactivation numbers since 2017, so a consistent finding has not yet been confirmed by anyone outside that original group.

Almost Nobody Actually Studied This Exact Parasite: only 16 of the 54 pieces of evidence (30%) tested Cyclospora cayetanensis itself. The other 38 (70%) studied a different pathogen entirely, such as E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria, or hepatitis E virus, or used Eimeria acervulina, a chicken parasite used as a stand-in because Cyclospora cannot currently be grown in a laboratory. That evidence can support the general idea that heat beats washing, but it cannot confirm the claim's exact numbers for this specific parasite.

We Do Not Always Know How Many Samples Were Tested: 35 of the 54 pieces of evidence (65%) list their sample size as "Not reported." DATOM's own scoring separately flags 45 of the 54 (83%) with a sample-size concern serious enough to question the result, including 9 pieces of evidence with so few samples that one unusual result could change the entire finding. Only 9 of the 54 (17%) are confirmed as adequately sized.

Very Few Studies Repeated Each Other's Methods: 44 different research methods appear across the 54 pieces of evidence, everything from microwave heating trials to computer simulations to household tap-water tests. That variety means almost nothing in this set gets independently confirmed by a second study using a comparably designed test.

We Cannot Always Check the Sources: 37 of the 54 pieces of evidence (69%), more than two thirds, are extracted as text summaries without the full original paper attached, versus 17 (31%) with the full paper reviewed. Journal information is missing for all 54, and one 1999 study from Nepal has no DOI on file at all, only a PubMed link. That means most of this evidence base is currently hard to independently double-check against the original document.

datoms.claim: Microwave heating inactivates Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts with measurable reduction in sporulation and viability.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Jye‐Yin Liao "Microwave Inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis Sporulation and Viability of Cryptosporidium parvum Oocysts" (2006). doi:10.4315/0362-028x-69.8.1957
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in laboratory culture
datoms.measure: Oocyst sporulation and viability reduction via microwave heating
datoms.methodology: In vitro thermal inactivation study
datoms.notes: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative efficacy data (log-reduction values or percentage inactivation) needed to directly compare against the nucleus claim's >99.9% (3-log) threshold.

datoms.claim: High hydrostatic pressure treatment of produce contaminated with Eimeria acervulina (a Cyclospora cayetanensis surrogate) achieves measurable inactivation of oocysts.
datoms.source: Kalmia E. Kniel, Adrienne E.H. Shearer, Jennifer L. Cascarino, G. C. Wilkins, Mark C. Jenkins "High Hydrostatic Pressure and UV Light Treatment of Produce Contaminated with Eimeria acervulina as a Cyclospora cayetanensis Surrogate" (2007). doi:10.4315/0362-028x-70.12.2837
datoms.population: Fresh produce contaminated with Eimeria acervulina oocysts
datoms.measure: Oocyst inactivation/reduction
datoms.methodology: Experimental treatment study with surrogate organism
datoms.notes: The study uses a surrogate organism rather than the target pathogen, which may not perfectly model Cyclospora cayetanensis response to treatments.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 70°C for 2 minutes does not achieve >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Clostridioides difficile spores in milk.
datoms.source: Gizem Taylan Yalçın, Melike Nur Tosun Demir, Nükhet Nilüfer Demirel Zorba "High thermal resistance and inactivation behaviour of Clostridioides difficile spores in milk." (2026). doi:10.1007/s42770-026-01975-z
datoms.population: Clostridioides difficile spores (strains and milk-derived isolates) in milk
datoms.measure: Log reduction of spore inactivation at specified temperatures and time intervals
datoms.methodology: Thermal inactivation kinetics study with log-linear, Weibull, and biphasic modeling
datoms.notes: The study focused on C. difficile spores in milk rather than fresh produce; results may not directly transfer to other food matrices or pathogens.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 70°C for 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Lucy J. Robertson "Assessing and Controlling the Risk of Cyclospora cayetanensis in the Food-Chain" (2017). doi:10.1007/978-3-319-53587-6_7
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh agricultural produce
datoms.measure: Log reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts following thermal processing
datoms.methodology: Laboratory thermal inactivation study
datoms.notes: The review synthesizes existing data; direct experimental validation across all produce varieties was not performed in this paper.

datoms.claim: Heating Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts to 70°C prevents sporulation (an indicator of viability) in basil and water substrates.
datoms.source: Lakshmi Sathyanarayanan, Ynés R. Ortega "EFFECTS OF TEMPERATURE AND DIFFERENT FOOD MATRICES ON CYCLOSPORA CAYETANENSIS OOCYST SPORULATION" (2006). doi:10.1645/ge-630r.1
datoms.population: Unsporulated Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in basil leaves and water
datoms.measure: Oocyst sporulation (viability indicator) after thermal exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro thermal inactivation with sporulation assay
datoms.notes: The paper does not report the exact duration of heating at 70°C, does not quantify inactivation as log-reductions, and does not test fresh produce varieties beyond basil or assess washing protocols.

datoms.claim: Heating Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts to 100°C prevents sporulation in basil and water substrates.
datoms.source: Lakshmi Sathyanarayanan, Ynés R. Ortega "EFFECTS OF TEMPERATURE AND DIFFERENT FOOD MATRICES ON CYCLOSPORA CAYETANENSIS OOCYST SPORULATION" (2006). doi:10.1645/ge-630r.1
datoms.population: Unsporulated Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in basil leaves and water
datoms.measure: Oocyst sporulation (viability indicator) after thermal exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro thermal inactivation with sporulation assay
datoms.notes: The paper does not report the exact duration of heating at 100°C, does not quantify inactivation as log-reductions, and does not test fresh produce varieties beyond basil or assess washing protocols.

datoms.claim: Heating C. cayetanensis oocysts to 70°C prevents sporulation of the parasite.
datoms.source: S. Almerı́a, Hediye Nese Cinar, J. P. Dubey "Cyclospora cayetanensis and Cyclosporiasis: An Update" (2019). doi:10.3390/microorganisms7090317
datoms.population: C. cayetanensis oocysts in water, basil, and dairy products
datoms.measure: Sporulation of C. cayetanensis oocysts after thermal exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro thermal inactivation study
datoms.notes: The paper is a review article and does not present original experimental data. The specific duration of heating at 70°C is not clearly stated for all matrices. The paper does not report quantitative measures of oocyst viability loss or log-reduction values.

datoms.claim: The paper studies inactivation of E. coli O157:H7, Salmonella enterica, and Listeria monocytogenes in coconut liquid endosperm, not Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce.
datoms.source: A. Gabriel, Jeffrey M. Ostonal, Jannelle O Cristobal, Gladess A. Pagal, John Vincent E Armada "Individual and combined efficacies of mild heat and ultraviolet-c radiation against Escherichia coli O157:H7, Salmonella enterica, and Listeria monocytogenes in coconut liquid endosperm." (2018). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2018.04.019
datoms.population: Bacterial cocktails in coconut liquid endosperm
datoms.measure: Log reduction of bacterial pathogens under heat and UV-C treatment
datoms.methodology: In vitro heat and UV-C inactivation kinetics study
datoms.notes: Study limited to three bacterial pathogens in a single liquid substrate; does not assess efficacy against parasitic oocysts or on whole fresh produce surfaces.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of fresh produce at sustained internal temperature of 70°C (158°F) for minimum 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts.
datoms.source: Linda S. Mansfield, Alvin A. Gajadhar "Cyclospora cayetanensis, a food- and waterborne coccidian parasite" (2004). doi:10.1016/j.vetpar.2004.09.011
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh agricultural produce
datoms.measure: Oocyst inactivation rate (log reduction)
datoms.methodology: Literature review and parasitology synthesis
datoms.notes: As a review article, this paper does not present original experimental data on thermal inactivation or washing protocols. Specific quantitative findings on the nucleus claim are not present in the provided text.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of fresh produce at 70°C (158°F) for 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Betty H. Olson "Cyclospora cayetanensis: a review of an emerging parasitic coccidian" (2003). doi:10.1016/s0020-7519(02)00268-0
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh agricultural produce
datoms.measure: Oocyst inactivation rate (log reduction)
datoms.methodology: Literature review and synthesis
datoms.notes: As a review article, findings are synthesized from existing literature rather than original experimental data; specific produce types and conditions may vary.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols (using laboratory detergent) can recover Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts from lettuce, herbs, and raspberries, indicating that oocysts remain on produce surfaces after washing.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Michelle Minjung Lee, Helen Murphy "Use of a common laboratory glassware detergent improves recovery of Cryptosporidium parvum and Cyclospora cayetanensis from lettuce, herbs and raspberries" (2011). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2011.10.025
datoms.population: Lettuce, herbs (unspecified varieties), and raspberries artificially contaminated with C. cayetanensis oocysts
datoms.measure: Recovery efficiency of C. cayetanensis oocysts from produce surfaces using detergent-based washing
datoms.methodology: Laboratory recovery and detection study
datoms.notes: The paper focuses on recovery methodology rather than quantifying the absolute reduction rates achieved by washing protocols or thermal processing.

datoms.claim: Elevated temperature alone (without high pressure) achieves log reductions in microbial populations, but the specific inactivation rate of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts at 70°C for 2 minutes is not quantified in this paper.
datoms.source: D. Wilson, L. Dabrowski, S. Stringer, R. Moezelaar, T. Brocklehurst "High pressure in combination with elevated temperature as a method for the sterilisation of food" (2008). doi:10.1016/J.TIFS.2008.01.005
datoms.population: Food sterilization systems (general)
datoms.measure: Microbial inactivation via thermal and high-pressure processing
datoms.methodology: Literature review and experimental design discussion
datoms.notes: The paper does not provide experimental data on Cyclospora cayetanensis oocyst inactivation at the specific temperature and duration stated in the nucleus claim.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of mozzarella curd at 90–95°C for 5–10 minutes achieves log reductions of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157 and O26 ranging from 1.01 to >5.38 log MPN/g, with higher reductions at higher core temperatures (78–80°C).
datoms.source: M. Trevisani, A. Valero, Rocco Mancusi "Effectiveness of the Thermal Treatments Used for Curd Stretching in the Inactivation of Shiga Toxin-Producing O157 and O26 Escherichia coli" (2017). doi:10.1155/2017/1609836
datoms.population: Mozzarella cheese curd artificially contaminated with E. coli O157:H7 and O26:H11
datoms.measure: Log reduction (log MPN/g) of viable Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157 and O26 after thermal treatment
datoms.methodology: Challenge test with nonisothermal temperature profiling
datoms.notes: Study was limited to mozzarella curd and two STEC serotypes. Temperature range studied was 64–80°C for O26 and 67–80°C for O157. Data on STEC growth during pre-stretching processing steps were lacking. Strain-dependent variability in heat resistance was not fully characterized.

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve a 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on basil.
datoms.source: Venessa Chandra, María P. Torres, Ynés R. Ortega "Efficacy of Wash Solutions in Recovering Cyclospora cayetanensis, Cryptosporidium parvum, and Toxoplasma gondii from Basil" (2014). doi:10.4315/0362-028x.jfp-13-381
datoms.population: Basil leaves artificially inoculated with Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts
datoms.measure: Percentage of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts recovered after washing with various solutions
datoms.methodology: Experimental wash efficacy study
datoms.notes: The study was limited to basil as a single produce type and used artificially inoculated oocysts rather than naturally contaminated produce.

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Lucy J. Robertson "Assessing and Controlling the Risk of Cyclospora cayetanensis in the Food-Chain" (2017). doi:10.1007/978-3-319-53587-6_7
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh agricultural produce
datoms.measure: Log reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts following washing protocols
datoms.methodology: Literature review and comparative analysis of washing efficacy
datoms.notes: The review does not present original experimental data on washing efficacy; conclusions are based on synthesis of existing literature.

datoms.claim: Washing vegetables does not completely remove Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts from produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Concepcion Roxas, Robert H. Gilman, Norma Miller, Lilia Cabrera "Isolation of Cryptosporidium parvum and Cyclospora cayetanensis from Vegetables Collected in Markets of an Endemic Region in Peru" (1997). doi:10.4269/ajtmh.1997.57.683
datoms.population: Vegetables collected from markets in periurban Peru
datoms.measure: Presence of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on vegetables after washing
datoms.methodology: Market vegetable sampling and microscopic examination
datoms.sample_size: Multiple vegetables from several markets across three time periods
datoms.notes: The study does not quantify the reduction percentage achieved by washing or compare washing efficacy to thermal processing. No specific log-reduction values are provided.

datoms.claim: Washing green leafy vegetables in distilled water does not achieve a 99% (2-log) or greater reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts.
datoms.source: Jeevan B. Sherchand, J. Helen Cross, Masamine Jimba, Shardulendra P. Sherchand, Milan Shrestha "Study of Cyclospora cayetanensis in health care facilities, sewage water and green leafy vegetables in Nepal." (1999)
datoms.population: Green leafy vegetables from Nepal
datoms.measure: Presence of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in vegetable washings
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional environmental sampling and microscopic examination
datoms.notes: The study does not quantify the number of oocysts or the percentage reduction achieved by washing. No comparison to thermal processing or other decontamination methods is provided. The study acknowledges that further studies are needed to clarify the direct link between these sources and infection.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols (commercial and consumer standard) fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Amy Mann, María P. Torres, Vitaliano Cama "Efficacy of Gaseous Chlorine Dioxide as a Sanitizer against Cryptosporidium parvum, Cyclospora cayetanensis, and Encephalitozoon intestinalis on Produce" (2008). doi:10.4315/0362-028x-71.12.2410
datoms.population: Fresh produce (lettuce, cilantro, berries) artificially contaminated with C. cayetanensis oocysts
datoms.measure: Log reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on produce after washing
datoms.methodology: Experimental contamination and washing trial
datoms.notes: Study used artificially inoculated produce rather than naturally contaminated samples; oocyst enumeration methods not fully detailed.

datoms.claim: Washing alone does not effectively remove C. cayetanensis oocysts from fresh produce.
datoms.source: S. Almerı́a, Hediye Nese Cinar, J. P. Dubey "Cyclospora cayetanensis and Cyclosporiasis: An Update" (2019). doi:10.3390/microorganisms7090317
datoms.population: Fresh produce (berries, leafy greens) contaminated with C. cayetanensis
datoms.measure: Effectiveness of washing in removing C. cayetanensis oocysts from produce
datoms.methodology: Literature review and epidemiological analysis
datoms.notes: This is a review article synthesizing published outbreak data. The paper does not present quantitative data on the efficacy of washing protocols or specific log-reduction values. The paper does not directly compare washing efficacy to thermal processing in controlled experiments.

datoms.claim: Commercial disinfectants show limited efficacy against Cryptosporidium oocysts.
datoms.source: Ayman Ahmed Shehata, Iqra Zafar, Hiroki Bochimoto, Kentaro Kato "The Synergistic Effect of Tanabesol and Calcium Hydroxide on Cryptosporidium parvum Oocyst Inactivation." (2026). doi:10.4103/IJVSM.IJVSM_11_25
datoms.population: Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts
datoms.measure: efficacy of commercial disinfectants against oocyst inactivation
datoms.methodology: Literature review and experimental assessment
datoms.notes: The paper does not provide specific quantitative efficacy data or comparative analysis with thermal processing methods.

datoms.claim: Sanitizer washing (free chlorine or peracetic acid) of fresh-cut Brassica vegetables reduces initial pathogen populations but does not achieve sustained multi-log inactivation over storage periods.
datoms.source: Nirosha Ruwani Amarasekara, Deepak Subedi, Joshua B Gurtler, Xuetong Fan "Effects of temperature and sanitizer wash treatments on foodborne pathogen survival during storage of work-in-process fresh-cut Brassica vegetables." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.fm.2026.105179
datoms.population: Work-in-process broccoli stalk, Brussels sprout, and kale inoculated with pathogen cocktails (ca. 8 log CFU/ml)
datoms.measure: Pathogen population reduction (log CFU/g) following sanitizer washing and storage
datoms.methodology: Experimental inoculation and sanitizer treatment study
datoms.notes: Study focused on three Brassica vegetables and three specific pathogens; generalizability to other produce types and pathogens not addressed. Storage duration limited to 7 days.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols using slightly acidic electrolysed water (SAEW) at 80 mg/L achieve a 4–8 log₁₀ CFU/g reduction in microbial load on whole tomatoes, mushrooms, carrots, and strawberries.
datoms.source: Harshveer Kaur, Juhi Saxena "Effect of slightly acidic electrolysed water, ozonated water and sodium hypochlorite wash on microbial and physico-chemical quality of whole tomatoes, mushrooms, carrots and strawberries." (2026). doi:10.1177/10820132261452148
datoms.population: Whole tomatoes, mushrooms, carrots, and strawberries stored at 4°C and 22°C
datoms.measure: Log₁₀ CFU/g microbial reduction (total plate count and E. coli)
datoms.methodology: In vitro microbial reduction assay with storage monitoring
datoms.notes: The paper does not report sample size, replication number, or statistical power. Study duration for storage monitoring is not explicitly stated. The study measures general microbial load, not pathogen-specific inactivation rates.

datoms.claim: Washing methods using vinegar or commercial benzalkonium chloride disinfectant achieve complete elimination of detectable Escherichia coli on fresh vegetables, whereas water, saline, and detergent show incomplete effectiveness.
datoms.source: Aziz Gharaei, M. Fasihi Karami, Mohammad Javad Boozhmehrani, M. Tavalla "Comparative Efficacy of Washing Methods for Bacterial and Parasitic Decontamination of Fresh Vegetables" (2026). doi:10.5812/jjnpp-170334
datoms.population: Seven varieties of fresh vegetables (lettuce, purslane, basil, mint, leek, radish, cress) sourced from retail outlets in Ahvaz, Iran
datoms.measure: Escherichia coli elimination and log CFU/g reduction following washing treatments
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional experimental study with culture-based bacterial detection
datoms.sample_size: 2 kg total vegetables comprising 3 independent retail samples per vegetable type (approximately 250-300 g each)
datoms.notes: Relatively small sample size and convenience sampling may limit generalizability. Parasitic identification relied on microscopy without molecular confirmation. Seasonal variation not evaluated. Single geographic region studied. Bacterial growth evaluated semi-quantitatively rather than by precise CFU enumeration.

datoms.claim: Parasitic contamination, particularly Giardia lamblia cysts, persists across all washing methods (11.1-33.3% prevalence) despite complete elimination of detectable E. coli by vinegar and commercial disinfectant treatments.
datoms.source: Aziz Gharaei, M. Fasihi Karami, Mohammad Javad Boozhmehrani, M. Tavalla "Comparative Efficacy of Washing Methods for Bacterial and Parasitic Decontamination of Fresh Vegetables" (2026). doi:10.5812/jjnpp-170334
datoms.population: Seven varieties of fresh vegetables (lettuce, purslane, basil, mint, leek, radish, cress) sourced from retail outlets in Ahvaz, Iran
datoms.measure: Giardia lamblia cyst persistence and prevalence following washing treatments
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional experimental study with sediment concentration microscopy for parasite detection
datoms.sample_size: 2 kg total vegetables comprising 3 independent retail samples per vegetable type (approximately 250-300 g each); 9 samples per washing treatment group
datoms.notes: Parasitic identification relied on microscopy without molecular confirmation, which may underestimate species diversity. Seasonal variation in contamination patterns not evaluated. Study conducted in single geographic region. Analytical approach designed to recover parasites dislodged into washing solution rather than assess parasite inactivation directly.

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh produce.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Betty H. Olson "Cyclospora cayetanensis: a review of an emerging parasitic coccidian" (2003). doi:10.1016/s0020-7519(02)00268-0
datoms.population: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh agricultural produce
datoms.measure: Oocyst removal/inactivation by washing (log reduction)
datoms.methodology: Literature review and synthesis
datoms.notes: As a review article, specific washing protocols and conditions are not uniformly detailed across cited studies; effectiveness may vary by produce type.

datoms.claim: Chemical washing protocols (chlorine at 170 ppm for 180 seconds or PAA at 70 ppm for 180 seconds) achieve log reductions of 0.9–2.3 on mung bean sprouts, falling short of the 2-log (99%) reduction threshold claimed for maximum standard washing protocols.
datoms.source: Shan Yu Neo, Pei Yan Lim, Li Kai Phua, Gek Hoon Khoo, Su-Jung Kim "Efficacy of chlorine and peroxyacetic acid on reduction of natural microflora, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Listeria monocyotgenes and Salmonella spp. on mung bean sprouts." (2013). doi:10.1016/j.fm.2013.05.001
datoms.population: Mung bean sprouts inoculated with E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, Salmonella spp., and natural microflora
datoms.measure: Log reduction of pathogens and natural microflora on sprouts after chemical sanitizer treatment
datoms.methodology: In vitro sanitizer efficacy trial
datoms.notes: Study limited to mung bean sprouts and specific bacterial pathogens; does not address parasitic pathogens like Cyclospora or thermal processing methods.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols using lactic acid (2%) combined with low-concentration sodium hypochlorite (4 mg/L) achieve approximately 1.77 log reduction of inoculated Listeria innocua on organic broccoli sprouts at day 0.
datoms.source: Lin Chen, Hongfei Zhang, Qin Liu, Xinyi Pang, Xue Zhao "Sanitising efficacy of lactic acid combined with low-concentration sodium hypochlorite on Listeria innocua in organic broccoli sprouts." (2019). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.02.014
datoms.population: Organic broccoli sprouts inoculated with Listeria innocua
datoms.measure: Log reduction (CFU/g fresh weight) of Listeria innocua on broccoli sprouts
datoms.methodology: In vitro antimicrobial efficacy trial on inoculated produce
datoms.notes: The study used Listeria innocua as a surrogate organism rather than pathogenic species. Results are specific to broccoli sprouts and may not generalize to other produce types. The study did not compare efficacy to thermal processing or standard commercial washing protocols.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure Cyclospora cayetanensis oocyst inactivation or washing protocol efficacy on fresh produce.
datoms.source: Chyer Kim, Rana Alrefaei, Mariam Bushlaibi, E. Ndegwa, P. Kaseloo "Influence of growth temperature on thermal tolerance of leading foodborne pathogens" (2019). doi:10.1002/fsn3.1268
datoms.population: Four bacterial species (E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, S. enterica, S. aureus) cultured in tryptic soy broth
datoms.measure: Thermal death time (D-value) and thermal death temperature (z-value) for bacterial pathogens
datoms.methodology: In vitro bacterial culture and thermal inactivation study
datoms.sample_size: 3 or 4 strains per bacterial species; 3 independent replicate trials per condition
datoms.notes: The study was conducted in laboratory broth (tryptic soy broth) rather than on actual food matrices. The authors note that further research is needed to validate findings on food matrices such as ground beef and roasted beef. The study did not assess thermal tolerance on fresh produce or compare washing protocols.

datoms.claim: Household washing of lettuce with tap water at 8 L/min flow rate achieves approximately 80% (0.9 log₁₀) reduction in total aerobic count, which is substantially less than the >99.9% (3-log) reduction claimed for thermal processing.
datoms.source: Elisabeth Uhlig, Crister Olsson, Jiayi He, Therese Stark, Zuzanna Sadowska "Effects of household washing on bacterial load and removal of Escherichia coli from lettuce and "ready-to-eat" salads." (2017). doi:10.1002/fsn3.514
datoms.population: Ready-to-eat mixed salad and romaine lettuce purchased from supermarket
datoms.measure: Total aerobic count reduction (log₁₀ CFU/g) after household tap water washing
datoms.methodology: Experimental bacterial culture and viable plate counting
datoms.notes: The study was limited to two washing procedures feasible under household conditions. Only a limited number of isolates were sequenced. The study did not assess thermal processing or Cyclospora oocysts.

datoms.claim: Household washing of lettuce with tap water at 2 L/min flow rate or by immersion in water does not achieve statistically significant reduction in bacterial load, failing to meet even a 99% (2-log) reduction threshold.
datoms.source: Elisabeth Uhlig, Crister Olsson, Jiayi He, Therese Stark, Zuzanna Sadowska "Effects of household washing on bacterial load and removal of Escherichia coli from lettuce and "ready-to-eat" salads." (2017). doi:10.1002/fsn3.514
datoms.population: Ready-to-eat mixed salad and romaine lettuce purchased from supermarket
datoms.measure: Total aerobic count and Enterobacteriaceae count reduction at low flow rate and immersion washing
datoms.methodology: Experimental bacterial culture and viable plate counting
datoms.notes: Study limited to two washing procedures feasible under household conditions. Did not assess thermal processing or other decontamination methods.

datoms.claim: Inoculated E. coli on romaine lettuce cannot be significantly reduced by household water immersion washing, even after five repeated 30-second immersions.
datoms.source: Elisabeth Uhlig, Crister Olsson, Jiayi He, Therese Stark, Zuzanna Sadowska "Effects of household washing on bacterial load and removal of Escherichia coli from lettuce and "ready-to-eat" salads." (2017). doi:10.1002/fsn3.514
datoms.population: Romaine lettuce inoculated with nonpathogenic E. coli CCUG 29300
datoms.measure: E. coli CFU/g reduction after repeated water immersion washing
datoms.methodology: Experimental bacterial inoculation and viable plate counting
datoms.sample_size: 6 separate heads of romaine lettuce (100 g per head)
datoms.notes: Study used nonpathogenic E. coli rather than pathogenic strains. Limited to immersion washing method for inoculated samples. Did not assess thermal processing.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure thermal processing or washing efficacy outcomes; it only detects C. cayetanensis DNA in produce and irrigation water using molecular methods.
datoms.source: Iffat Naz, Mina A. Almayouf, Abdul Rehman, Abdul Majid, Abdul Basit "Molecular detection of Cyclospora cayetanensis in fresh produce and irrigation water in peri- urban settings: a One Health cross-sectional study" (2026). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9256916/v1
datoms.population: Fresh produce (coriander, mint, lettuce, spinach, cucumber, tomato) and irrigation water from peri-urban Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
datoms.measure: Presence/absence of C. cayetanensis DNA detected by nested PCR targeting 18S rRNA gene
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional molecular survey with nested PCR
datoms.sample_size: 300 produce samples and 120 irrigation water samples (420 total)
datoms.notes: Study did not measure thermal inactivation or washing efficacy. Molecular detection sensitivity may be reduced by complex sample matrices and PCR inhibitors. Seasonal sampling duration was limited. Results not directly comparable with microscopy-based reports due to methodological differences.

datoms.claim: The BAM 19b method achieves detection of C. cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce at a sensitivity of 100% when 200 oocysts are spiked onto berries.
datoms.source: Laura F. Lalonde, Jenna R. Oakley, Patrick Fries "Verification and Use of the US-FDA BAM 19b Method for Detection of Cyclospora cayetanensis in a Survey of Fresh Produce by CFIA Laboratory" (2022). doi:10.3390/microorganisms10030559
datoms.population: Fresh berries (raspberries, strawberries, blueberries) spiked with C. cayetanensis oocysts
datoms.measure: Diagnostic sensitivity (percentage of spiked samples positive by qPCR)
datoms.methodology: Laboratory spiking and qPCR verification study
datoms.notes: Lower sensitivity at lower spike levels compared to FDA validation; oocyst stock was only 4% sporulated; use of different amplification platform than original FDA validation.

datoms.claim: The BAM 19b method achieves detection of C. cayetanensis oocysts in leafy greens at a sensitivity of 92.5% when 200 oocysts are spiked onto samples.
datoms.source: Laura F. Lalonde, Jenna R. Oakley, Patrick Fries "Verification and Use of the US-FDA BAM 19b Method for Detection of Cyclospora cayetanensis in a Survey of Fresh Produce by CFIA Laboratory" (2022). doi:10.3390/microorganisms10030559
datoms.population: Fresh leafy greens (romaine lettuce, spring mix, kale salad mix, coleslaw) spiked with C. cayetanensis oocysts
datoms.measure: Diagnostic sensitivity (percentage of spiked samples positive by qPCR)
datoms.methodology: Laboratory spiking and qPCR verification study
datoms.notes: Lower sensitivity at lower spike levels; oocyst stock was only 4% sporulated; differences in oocyst preparation procedures compared to FDA validation.

datoms.claim: UV radiation at 222, 254, and 282 nm significantly reduces the infectivity of Eimeria acervulina oocysts, achieving reductions ranging from 82% to >99.6% (0.76-log to near 3-log) in oocyst shedding when administered to chickens.
datoms.source: Aaron A. Baumann, Addison K Myers, Niloofar Khajeh-Kazerooni, Ashley Wise-Mitchell, Benjamin M. Rosenthal "UV radiation at 222, 254, and 282 nm inhibits sporulation and suppresses infectivity of Eimeria acervulina oocysts" (2025). doi:10.1128/spectrum.02439-24
datoms.population: 2-week-old broiler chickens (HR308 strain), n=3 per treatment group
datoms.domain: Parasitology; food safety; UV disinfection; poultry disease
datoms.measure: Oocyst shedding (oocyst output per chicken) measured from fecal material collected days 5–7 post-inoculation
datoms.methodology: In vivo infectivity assay in broiler chickens
datoms.sample_size: 3 chickens per treatment group; 500 oocysts per chicken inoculation
datoms.notes: The study used a relatively low inoculation dose (500 oocysts) to allow comparison of oocyst fecundity without causing clinical signs such as intestinal lesions. Results may not generalize to higher infection doses or to natural transmission routes. The study was conducted in controlled laboratory conditions and does not account for real-world barriers to UV penetration in complex matrices.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at ≥63°C for ≥5 minutes or ≥75°C for 5 minutes achieves effective inactivation of hepatitis E virus (HEV), with reductions >4 log₁₀ in genomic titre.
datoms.source: Audrey Fraisse, Marie Pellerin, Carole Feurer, Jean-Luc Martin, Virginie Doceul "Optimization of a capsid integrity RT-qPCR method to quantify thermally inactivated hepatitis E virus in suspensions and in deli meat samples." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.fm.2026.105193
datoms.population: HEV-3c and HEV-3f strains in PBS, cell culture medium, cooked ham, and emulsified sausage
datoms.measure: Log₁₀ reduction in HEV genomic titre and infectivity
datoms.methodology: Capsid-integrity RT-qPCR and cell culture assay
datoms.notes: The study focused on HEV-3 strains in specific food matrices (cooked ham and emulsified sausage). Further validation is needed for other HEV genotypes and complex food matrices.

datoms.claim: Acid adaptation increases the thermal heat resistance of Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, and STEC in fruit juices.
datoms.source: Zeynal Topalcengiz "Assessment of recommended thermal inactivation parameters for fruit juices" (2019). doi:10.1016/J.LWT.2019.108475
datoms.population: STEC, Salmonella, and L. monocytogenes strains
datoms.measure: Heat resistance of acid-adapted versus non-adapted bacteria
datoms.methodology: Experimental heat treatment with acid-adapted and non-adapted bacterial strains
datoms.notes: The study focused on juice rather than whole produce. The specific magnitude of increased heat resistance was not quantified.

datoms.claim: Thermal treatment at 60°C for 2 minutes achieves a 3.3–4.0 log reduction (99.97–99.99% inactivation) of Salmonella enterica populations in vitro.
datoms.source: A. Gill, S. Tamber, Xianqin Yang "Relative response of populations of Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica to exposure to thermal, alkaline and acidic treatments." (2019). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.01.007
datoms.population: Salmonella enterica strains (n=99) from humans, poultry, pork, and beef sources
datoms.measure: Log reduction (CFU/mL) of Salmonella enterica after heat exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro bacterial culture exposure to thermal treatment
datoms.notes: Study used a model system with bacterial cultures in broth rather than on actual food matrices; results may not directly translate to produce or other food types.

datoms.claim: Thermal treatment at 60°C for 2 minutes achieves a 3.3–3.5 log reduction (99.9–99.97% inactivation) of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli populations in vitro.
datoms.source: A. Gill, S. Tamber, Xianqin Yang "Relative response of populations of Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica to exposure to thermal, alkaline and acidic treatments." (2019). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.01.007
datoms.population: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strains (n=113) from cattle, beef, and human sources
datoms.measure: Log reduction (CFU/mL) of STEC after heat exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro bacterial culture exposure to thermal treatment
datoms.notes: Study used bacterial cultures in broth rather than on actual food matrices; results may not directly translate to produce or other food types.

datoms.claim: Thermal treatment at 60°C for 2 minutes achieves a 2.3–3.8 log reduction (99.8–99.98% inactivation) of generic E. coli populations in vitro.
datoms.source: A. Gill, S. Tamber, Xianqin Yang "Relative response of populations of Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica to exposure to thermal, alkaline and acidic treatments." (2019). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.01.007
datoms.population: Generic E. coli strains (n=99) from beef carcasses and trim at small and large processing plants
datoms.measure: Log reduction (CFU/mL) of generic E. coli after heat exposure
datoms.methodology: In vitro bacterial culture exposure to thermal treatment
datoms.notes: Study used bacterial cultures in broth rather than on actual food matrices; results may not directly translate to produce or other food types.

datoms.claim: Ohmic heating of poultry meat can achieve bacterial inactivation of foodborne pathogens including Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli, and Campylobacter, with inactivation probability dependent on applied voltage, brine concentration, and processing time.
datoms.source: Sebahattin Serhat Turgut, A. H. Feyissa "Stochastic inactivation evaluation of foodborne pathogens during ohmic heating of poultry meat" (2023). doi:10.1515/ijfe-2023-0022
datoms.population: Chicken meat samples with 1000 virtual bacterial particles
datoms.measure: Probability of 7-log bacterial reduction during ohmic heating
datoms.methodology: Computational fluid dynamics modeling with stochastic simulation
datoms.notes: Model represents virtual bacterial particles rather than actual microbial behavior; validation against experimental data not reported in abstract.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 75°C achieves measurable but limited inactivation of fungal spores in strawberry puree, with thermal processing alone at 85°C producing only 0.2 log reduction of B. nivea ascospores over 10 minutes.
datoms.source: Evelyn, Filipa V. M. Silva "Inactivation of Byssochlamys nivea ascospores in strawberry puree by high pressure, power ultrasound and thermal processing." (2015). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2015.07.031
datoms.population: B. nivea ascospores (four week old) in strawberry puree
datoms.measure: Log reduction of B. nivea ascospores
datoms.methodology: Experimental inactivation study with thermal processing and high pressure processing
datoms.notes: The study used strawberry puree rather than whole fresh produce, and examined B. nivea ascospores rather than Cyclospora oocysts. The paper does not address washing protocols or compare thermal processing to washing effectiveness.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of tomato juice and sauce at 80°C achieves measurable inactivation of Alicyclobacillus acidoterrestris spores, with D-values (decimal reduction time) of approximately 3.8-fold lower when combined with UV-C compared to heat alone.
datoms.source: Rose Daphnee Tchonkouang, Ferruh Erdogdu, Maria Dulce Antunes, Margarida Cortês Vieira "Quality and safety of reformulated tomato products processed by continuous heat and UV-C pasteurization." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.foodres.2026.119247
datoms.population: Reformulated tomato juice (RTJ; pH 3.70 ± 0.06, °Brix 5.27 ± 0.21) and reformulated tomato sauce (RTS; pH 4.04 ± 0.02, °Brix 7.96 ± 0.16)
datoms.measure: D-value and z-value for Alicyclobacillus acidoterrestris spore inactivation at 80°C
datoms.methodology: Kinetic modeling with Paired Equivalent Isothermal Exposures method
datoms.notes: Study limited to two reformulated tomato products (juice and sauce); does not assess fresh whole produce or Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts specifically.

datoms.claim: Dual-frequency acoustic cavitation combined with mild heat (50–55 °C) achieves a 3.6-log reduction in yeast after 450 seconds of treatment in apple juice.
datoms.source: Sara Maghami, Kimmo Rumpunen, Örjan Johansson "Reduced-temperature pasteurization of apple juice using a flow-through sonicator." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.ultsonch.2026.107926
datoms.population: Apple juice (Ingrid Marie variety)
datoms.measure: Log reduction of yeast, mold, and aerobic microorganisms
datoms.methodology: Flow-through sonication with dual-frequency acoustic and hydrodynamic cavitation
datoms.notes: Pure thermal pasteurization controls were not performed at the same temperature ranges; however, all treatment temperatures were below 60 °C, where thermal pasteurization alone is not expected to produce substantial microbial inactivation under comparable processing times. The study did not explicitly address how suspended solids and dissolved macromolecules in complex juice matrices modulate cavitation behavior. Bubbly apple juice acoustic properties were approximated using bubbly-water parameters in the absence of direct data.

datoms.claim: Treatment at 50–55 °C with dual-frequency acoustic cavitation achieves microbial inactivation exceeding 99.9% (3-log reduction) for yeast in apple juice, whereas lower temperatures (30–40 °C) fail to achieve measurable reduction.
datoms.source: Sara Maghami, Kimmo Rumpunen, Örjan Johansson "Reduced-temperature pasteurization of apple juice using a flow-through sonicator." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.ultsonch.2026.107926
datoms.population: Apple juice (Ingrid Marie variety)
datoms.measure: Presence or absence of microbial reduction trend across temperature ranges
datoms.methodology: Flow-through sonication with dual-frequency acoustic and hydrodynamic cavitation
datoms.notes: Pure thermal pasteurization controls were not performed at the same temperature ranges. All treatment temperatures were below 60 °C, where thermal pasteurization alone is not expected to produce substantial microbial inactivation. The study did not systematically isolate the individual contributions of temperature versus acoustic cavitation intensity.

datoms.claim: Thermal treatment at 71°C for 6 seconds in apple juice achieves a 5-log reduction of Salmonella.
datoms.source: Zeynal Topalcengiz "Assessment of recommended thermal inactivation parameters for fruit juices" (2019). doi:10.1016/J.LWT.2019.108475
datoms.population: Salmonella strains (non-adapted and acid-adapted)
datoms.measure: Log reduction of Salmonella viability
datoms.methodology: Experimental heat treatment in microcapillary tubes
datoms.notes: The study focused on juice rather than whole produce. Results are specific to the bacterial strains and adaptation conditions tested. Applicability to other produce types or processing conditions is not addressed.

datoms.claim: Thermal treatment at 71°C for 6-12 seconds in orange juice achieves a 5-log reduction of STEC.
datoms.source: Zeynal Topalcengiz "Assessment of recommended thermal inactivation parameters for fruit juices" (2019). doi:10.1016/J.LWT.2019.108475
datoms.population: STEC strains (non-adapted and acid-adapted)
datoms.measure: Log reduction of STEC viability
datoms.methodology: Experimental heat treatment in microcapillary tubes
datoms.notes: The study focused on juice rather than whole produce. Results are specific to the bacterial strains and adaptation conditions tested.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 90–98°C for 2.5–5 minutes reduces total mesophilic aerobic counts in mixed fruit and vegetable pulps by >2 log₁₀ cycles.
datoms.source: E. Gonçalves, I. Raposo, J. Pinheiro, Carla Alegria, Margarida Moldão "Quality changes during thermal processing of two mixed formulas of fruits and vegetables pulps" (2020). doi:10.9755/ejfa.2020.v32.i4.2093
datoms.population: Mixed fruit and vegetable pulps (pineapple, beetroot, strawberry, lemon juice, pear-based)
datoms.measure: Total mesophilic aerobic counts (TAPC) reduction in log₁₀ cycles
datoms.methodology: Thermal degradation kinetics study with time-temperature intervals
datoms.notes: The study focused on mixed fruit and vegetable pulps rather than whole fresh produce; microbial reduction was measured as total mesophilic aerobic counts rather than pathogen-specific inactivation; Cyclospora cayetanensis was not specifically evaluated.

datoms.claim: Micro-nano bubble treatment via high-speed vortex and ultrasound reduces microbial counts on lettuce and cherry tomatoes by 2.09 and 2.90 log CFU·g⁻¹, respectively.
datoms.source: Xiaolan Li, Yan Dong, Jiangning Shen, Lingzhi Zhang, Xianli Gao "Synergistic micro-nano bubble treatment via high-speed vortex and ultrasound enhances quality and safety of lettuce and cherry tomatoes." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.foodres.2026.119672
datoms.population: Lettuce and cherry tomatoes (fresh produce)
datoms.measure: Microbial count reduction (log CFU·g⁻¹)
datoms.methodology: Experimental treatment comparison with microbial enumeration
datoms.notes: The paper does not specify which microbial species were targeted or reduced, and does not measure Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts specifically.

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of meat products at temperatures achieving 'done' preparation results in log reductions of Escherichia coli ranging from 5–9 depending on product type, whereas 'rare' and 'medium' preparations achieve only 1–4 log reductions.
datoms.source: M. Pesciaroli, J. Chardon, E.H.M. Delfgou, A.F.A. Kuijpers, L. Wijnands "Home style frying of steak and meat products: Survival of Escherichia coli related to dynamic temperature profiles." (2019). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2019.03.020
datoms.population: Beefsteak, hamburgers (beef and 50% beef/50% pork), meatballs (beef and mixed), and crumbs inoculated with Escherichia coli O111:H2
datoms.domain: Food microbiology; quantitative microbial risk assessment
datoms.measure: Log reduction (inactivation) of Escherichia coli O111:H2 during home-style frying at different doneness levels
datoms.methodology: Experimental thermal inactivation with dynamic temperature profiling
datoms.notes: Limited measurements for some conditions; large variability in product properties and preparation styles in real life; further studies needed to analyze effect on survival and determine essential variables.

scope: Lab studies of produce, juice, and dairy treated with heat, washing, UV, or sanitizers
metric: Percent or log reduction of oocysts or bacteria, or whether they can still sporulate
